title: Sánchez’s biggest gamble yet – European Council on Foreign Relations
gist: A housing-crisis eviction in Madrid triggered nationwide protests; after Congress rejected two emergency housing decrees on October 2nd, Pedro Sánchez dissolved parliament and called a snap election for November 29th. Polls point toward a PP–Vox coalition that would bring the far right into Spanish government for the first time since the return of democracy, with a housing general strike set for November 11th.

insights.claim: The late-September eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid flat she had lived in for seven decades sparked nationwide protests over Spain's housing crisis.
insights.speaker: Carla Hobbs, Mark Leonard, José Ignacio Torreblanca
insights.so_what: Housing affordability has become a mass-mobilisation issue in Spain, raising the odds of interventionist housing and rental policy regardless of who governs.
insights.quote: In late September, 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from the Madrid flat she had lived in for seven decades, sparking nationwide protests over Spain’s housing crisis.

insights.claim: Spanish Congress rejected two emergency housing decrees from Pedro Sánchez's government on October 2nd, showing the minority government could not pass its housing response.
insights.speaker: Carla Hobbs, Mark Leonard, José Ignacio Torreblanca
insights.so_what: Legislative gridlock on housing means policy uncertainty for Spanish residential real estate and landlords persists until after the election.
insights.quote: Pedro Sánchez’s government responded with two emergency housing decrees which Congress rejected on October 2nd.

insights.claim: Spain's trade unions have called a general strike over housing for November 11th, weeks before the snap general election.
insights.speaker: Carla Hobbs, Mark Leonard, José Ignacio Torreblanca
insights.so_what: A housing-focused general strike could disrupt economic activity and keep housing at the centre of the campaign.
insights.quote: Spain’s trade unions have called a general strike over housing for November 11th, just weeks before the vote.

insights.claim: Three days after Congress rejected his housing decrees, Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez dissolved parliament and called a snap election for November 29th.
insights.speaker: Carla Hobbs, Mark Leonard, José Ignacio Torreblanca
insights.so_what: A late-November Spanish election is a near-term event risk for Spanish bonds, banks and housing-exposed equities.
insights.quote: Three days later, the prime minister dissolved parliament and called for a snap election on November 29th.

insights.claim: Pedro Sánchez has previously recovered from apparently losing positions, so the snap election is framed as a gamble that could still pay off despite unfavourable polls.
insights.speaker: Carla Hobbs, Mark Leonard, José Ignacio Torreblanca
insights.so_what: Markets should not fully price a change of government; Sánchez's track record of comebacks leaves outcome uncertainty high.
insights.quote: Sánchez has snatched victory from the jaws of defeat before

themes.theme: Far right's path to power in Spain

insights.claim: Polls ahead of Spain's November 29th election point toward a PP–Vox coalition, which would bring the far right into Spanish government for the first time since the return of democracy.
insights.speaker: Carla Hobbs, Mark Leonard, José Ignacio Torreblanca
insights.so_what: A PP–Vox government would shift Spain's fiscal, migration and EU stance, and add Spain to the list of European governments including the far right.
insights.quote: the polls are pointing towards a PP–Vox coalition that could bring the far right into government for the first time since the return of democracy.

source_meta.author: Carla Hobbs, Mark Leonard, José Ignacio Torreblanca
